stem: A head coach asks for "better scouting summaries" from a new Claude feature. The project lead must turn this into an acceptance criterion the team can test before launch. Which criterion best fits?

options.text: At least 95% of stat claims match source data on a 200-game eval set.
options.explanation: Correct. This criterion is specific and measurable and has a deadline, so it can become an eval and a pass/fail gate.

options.text: Summaries should be high quality, accurate and fast enough to keep the coaching staff satisfied.
options.explanation: These words describe goals, but nothing here can be measured or tested as written.

options.text: Summaries must use the most capable Claude model available.
options.explanation: This names a design choice, not an outcome. It doesn't say what a good summary is.

options.text: Coaches should report that they like the new summaries better than the old manual versions.
options.explanation: Opinion is useful feedback, but without a metric and test set it isn't a testable acceptance criterion.

stem: An insurer is writing requirements for a claims-intake assistant built on Claude. The analyst must separate functional requirements from infrastructure (non-functional) ones. Which TWO of these are infrastructure requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Extract the policy number, claim date and claim amount from each uploaded form.
options.explanation: This describes what the system must do with the input, so it's a functional requirement.

options.text: All model inference for claim data must run on US-based infrastructure.
options.explanation: Correct. Where processing happens is a constraint on how the system runs, which makes it an infrastructure requirement.

options.text: Flag any claim above the policy's coverage limit for human review.
options.explanation: This is a behavior the system must perform, so it's functional.

options.text: The first token of each assistant reply must appear within two seconds at the 95th percentile.
options.explanation: Correct. Latency targets constrain how the system performs rather than what it does, so they're non-functional.

options.text: Return each extracted claim as JSON that the existing claims system can ingest.
options.explanation: The output format is part of what the system must produce, so it's a functional requirement.

stem: A league office is building a fan-feedback analyzer on the Claude API. A legal review adds a hard requirement: model inference on fan messages must happen only in the United States. Which design choice satisfies this requirement?

options.text: Use a smaller model, since those are always served in the US.
options.explanation: Model size doesn't determine where inference runs. Geography is controlled separately.

options.text: Add a system-prompt instruction telling Claude to process fan messages only in the United States.
options.explanation: The model has no control over where it is served. A prompt can't enforce data location.

options.text: Set inference_geo to "us" on each request or as the workspace default.
options.explanation: Correct. inference_geo controls where inference runs, and the default is global. The workspace geo separately governs data at rest.

options.text: Enable zero data retention, which keeps all processing inside the customer's home region.
options.explanation: ZDR is about retention, not location. It doesn't pin inference to a geography.

stem: A retail company's requirement for an email classifier reads: "Lowest cost that achieves at least 95% accuracy on our labeled set." The engineering team defaults to the most capable model available. Which approach best fits the requirement?

options.text: Use the most capable model to give the team a safety margin.
options.explanation: The requirement asks for the cheapest model that passes, not the strongest. Extra capability adds cost the requirement doesn't call for.

options.text: Evaluate candidate models on the labeled set and pick the cheapest that reaches 95%.
options.explanation: Correct. Measuring candidates against the stated threshold and picking the least expensive passer meets both halves of the requirement.

options.text: Use the smallest model available, since cost is the first constraint listed in the requirement.
options.explanation: The cheapest model may miss the accuracy threshold. Both constraints have to hold.

options.text: Pick a model from a public benchmark leaderboard rather than spending time on internal evals.
options.explanation: Public benchmarks don't measure this company's emails. The requirement names its own labeled set.

stem: A team designed a game-recap service around a newly launched API feature on the first-party Claude API. Late in planning, procurement states that all spend must go through the company's existing AWS account. Which next step best fits?

options.text: Proceed as designed, since every Claude feature is available identically on all platforms.
options.explanation: Feature availability differs by platform, so assuming parity risks building on something the required platform lacks.

options.text: Keep the first-party API and defer procurement's constraint.
options.explanation: Procurement is a hard constraint from the architecture. Deferring it means the design will be rejected later.

options.text: Have one engineer pay for the first-party API with a personal key until procurement catches up.
options.explanation: Personal billing violates the procurement requirement and creates security and ownership problems.

options.text: Verify the feature exists on the AWS options before committing, and record why.
options.explanation: Correct. A stated platform constraint usually decides the item. Verifying availability first and recording why keeps the design traceable.

stem: A bank's customer-facing chat assistant has this requirement: users must see the response begin within two seconds, even when answers run to several paragraphs. Which design lever most directly addresses it?

options.text: Stream the response so text appears as it is generated, rather than after it finishes.
options.explanation: Correct. Streaming delivers the first tokens almost immediately, which directly addresses time to first visible output.

options.text: Process the chat requests through the Message Batches API to lower their cost.
options.explanation: Batches are asynchronous and suit work nobody is waiting on. They would make interactive latency far worse.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so long answers are never cut off before they finish.
options.explanation: A higher output cap doesn't make the response start sooner.

options.text: Require the most capable model so answers are complete on the first attempt.
options.explanation: A larger model is usually slower to respond. It doesn't help a time-to-first-output target.

stem: A media monitoring firm expects peak traffic of many concurrent requests that share the same 50,000-token system prompt, followed by a short article each. Load tests show 429 errors from the input-tokens-per-minute limit. The firm wants to meet throughput without moving to a higher tier yet. Which change best fits?

options.text: Raise concurrency so requests finish sooner and the per-minute window resets faster.
options.explanation: The limit uses a continuously refilling token bucket, so more concurrency just consumes it faster and causes more 429s.

options.text: Split each request into several smaller ones so no single request carries the full system prompt.
options.explanation: Each split request would still need the instructions, so total input tokens stay the same or grow.

options.text: Cache the shared system prompt, since cache reads mostly don't count toward that limit.
options.explanation: Correct. With prompt caching, only uncached input tokens count toward ITPM on most models, so a large shared prefix stops consuming most of the limit.

options.text: Raise max_tokens so that each response does more work and fewer requests are needed.
options.explanation: Output length has no bearing on the input-tokens limit, and longer outputs consume output-token capacity instead.

stem: A sports-betting operator wants Claude to draft weekly odds commentary that a trading desk publishes. In a requirements workshop, the analyst wants questions whose answers will set the guardrail and human-review requirements. Which TWO questions best fit? (Select TWO.)

options.text: What happens if a commentary contains a wrong number, and who is harmed by it?
options.explanation: Correct. The consequence of a wrong output sets how much checking and guardrailing the system needs.

options.text: Which Claude model version does the trading desk prefer to use for drafting?
options.explanation: Model choice follows from requirements. A stakeholder preference doesn't define review or guardrail needs.

options.text: Would the desk like the assistant to use the newest API features available?
options.explanation: Feature novelty is a solution choice, not a requirement, and says nothing about risk.

options.text: How many words should each commentary be on average across the season?
options.explanation: Length is a functional detail of the output, not a driver of review or safety controls.

options.text: Who must approve a commentary before publication, and within what time window?
options.explanation: Correct. Approval ownership and timing directly define the human-in-the-loop requirement.

stem: A finance team needs five fields extracted from vendor invoices into JSON every day. The steps never change, and each invoice is a single document. A developer proposes an autonomous multi-agent system with planning and web browsing. Which design best fits the requirements?

options.text: Build the multi-agent system, since it can adapt if invoice formats change in the future.
options.explanation: This adds cost, latency and failure modes for flexibility that the stated requirements don't ask for.

options.text: Give an agent computer-use tools so it can open each invoice in a desktop viewer.
options.explanation: Driving a GUI is slow and fragile when the document can be passed to the model directly.

options.text: Use a single model call per invoice with structured outputs, and validate the JSON before storing it.
options.explanation: Correct. A fixed, single-document extraction fits one call with a schema. That's the simplest design that meets the requirements.

options.text: Fine-tune a custom model on past invoices before building anything else.
options.explanation: This is heavy upfront work with no evidence that a prompted call with a schema falls short.

stem: A league office wants weekly recaps of all 300 games produced by the most capable model and also caps spending at a fixed weekly budget. A cost model shows that the two requirements can't both be met. Which next step best fits sound requirements practice?

options.text: Quietly switch to a cheaper model to meet the budget, since staying within cost is usually what matters.
options.explanation: Silently dropping a stated requirement breaks traceability and surprises stakeholders later.

options.text: Raise the conflict with stakeholders, let them prioritize, and record the decision.
options.explanation: Correct. Requirement conflicts should be raised early and resolved by the owners, with the decision traced to data and recorded.

options.text: Ship with the most capable model and ask for more budget once overspending has been demonstrated.
options.explanation: Knowingly breaking a constraint and fixing it afterwards isn't requirements management.

options.text: Drop the budget, because quality always outranks cost.
options.explanation: No rule says quality always wins. Priorities belong to the stakeholders who own the outcome.
